references.text: In [ref:Luk 15:21|Luke 15:21], the younger son repeats the words he had prepared: "I am no longer worthy to be called your son." This is the actual fulfillment of the confession he planned in verse 19.
[ref:Luk 15:18|Luke 15:18] is the immediate context where the son decides to return to his father and confess his sin – it is the beginning of the speech he prepares, which continues in verse 19.
In [ref:Luk 5:8|Luke 5:8], Simon Peter says: "Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man." The same sense of unworthiness before God as the prodigal son expresses to his father.
In [ref:1 Mos 32:10|Genesis 32:10], Jacob says: "I am not worthy of all the kindness and faithfulness you have shown your servant." A similar confession of unworthiness before God's grace.
In [ref:2 Sam 9:8|2 Samuel 9:8], Mephibosheth calls himself "a dead dog" and asks what he is worthy of – an expression of deep humility that recalls the prodigal son's self-abasement.
In [ref:Luk 7:6-7|Luke 7:6-7], the officer from Capernaum says he is not worthy for Jesus to come under his roof. The Greek word ἄξιος (worthy) is used here in the same way as in Luke 15:19.
In [ref:Matt 3:11|Matthew 3:11], John the Baptist says he is not worthy (ἱκανός) to carry the sandals of the one coming after him – a similar attitude of humility and unworthiness.
In [ref:Luk 3:16|Luke 3:16], John the Baptist expresses his unworthiness: he is not even worthy to untie his sandals. A parallel to the prodigal son's feeling of not deserving his position.
In [ref:Job 7:17|Job 7:17], Job asks: "What is man, that you make so much of him?" A similar question about human worth and standing before God.
In [ref:Sal 8:5|Psalm 8:5], the psalmist asks: "What is man – that you remember him?" This touches on the same theme of human unworthiness in relation to God's greatness.
